 How Adil Rashid fell out of England ODI favour... and how he could still get back in
 Katya Witney
 Nov 20, 2026 5 minute read News Share Share Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on WhatsApp Copy Link Close Harry Brook managed to dodge the hard questions about Adil Rashid’s absence during the ODI tri-series in Pakistan.
 His reasons were varied. Conditions weren’t suited to wrist-spinners – the only wicket taken by a leggie during the series was the one Rashid took in England’s opening game – and the benefit of Liam Dawson’s ability to pad out an inconsistent batting unit on run-scoring pitches was clear. However, having decided to leave Rashid out of the opening game in Australia as well, Brook outlined the reality of England’s ODI spin outlook.
 "Everybody knows how good Rash is,” said Brook . “He's a magician with the ball. He can tear through sides, and the skill that he possesses is unbelievable. It's awesome to have him in and around the squad.
 "But Liam Dawson did an exceptional job in Pakistan, and he did the role very well. He had a lot of clarity at the top of his mark, he knew exactly what he needed to do, and he performed well."
 The subtext was clear. Having spent a decade as England’s No.1 white-ball spinner, Rashid has started to drift into a peripheral figure.
 That gradual fade has been happening for almost a year, although it’s only now that it’s been openly addressed. Rashid was England’s leading wicket-taker during their series win in Sri Lanka last winter, and it was Dawson who dropped out when an extra pacer was required against India over the summer. But even as the sole specialist spinner, Rashid didn’t bowl his full quota of overs once during that series and was uncharacteristically expensive, returning an economy rate of 7.2.
 When he injured his hand for the following series against Sri Lanka, England turned to first Rehan Ahmed and then Dawson, allowing them to get four pacers in their XI, while, in theory, only minimally compromising on batting depth. In the final match of that series, Dawson took 3-26 from eight overs. When he was preferred over Rashid in the Pakistan tri-series , Dawson made the most of his opportunity once again, bowling his full quota in all three games and finishing as England’s leading wicket-taker. Despite taking four-for against Western Australia in a warm-up match in Perth, the writing has been on the wall for Rashid since England landed Down Under.
 Nevertheless, a divide has emerged over his sidelining, with opposition chiefly from those who have benefited the most from Rashid’s prowess.
 Speaking on For The Love Of Cricket podcast, Jos Buttler said: "Numerous times, I've said how Adil's the most important player that I've played with in those white-ball teams. I know time doesn't stand still for anyone, and everyone at some point is going to have a drop-off and curve [downwards]. Adil's an older player now, and has been so good for so long, and he won't be at that level forever.
 “But I think for us as a team to win that World Cup, Adil Rashid has to be there and be near his best. He's that important.”
 It’s revealing that, as a former captain and current player in Brook’s white-ball group – albeit an injured one – Buttler has weighed in on a selection call. Perhaps it’s reflective of his own position which, given he’s expected to be out of action until at least next summer, could be uncertain for next year’s World Cup. Or maybe it’s that Buttler feels strongly that his best chance of lifting another trophy is with Rashid by his side too.
 There’s also an interesting dimension to the assumption that Rashid’s age has led to a drop in form or his ousting from the core group. Dawson is only two years younger than Rashid, and given Rashid plays such little cricket outside of international series’, concerns over his workload are minimal. While fading out an ageing force may have played some part in the decision, more prescient is the prospect of a World Cup in South Africa, where teams will want to fit more pacers in. Also relevant is England’s inconsistent batting unit. With Dawson, England can pick three pacers as a minimum without compromising on batting depth.
 Equally, Brook’s assertion that England are looking for greater control in the middle overs doesn’t quite stack up. “If you look at the best teams in the world, that [middle overs] is the key area they're dominating at the minute,” said Brook. “That's something that we've spoken about a lot over the last week or so. We want to try to control those middle overs with bat and ball a little bit better than what we have. That could be being boring for a little period of time, or deciding to accelerate at some points.”
 Rashid has been England’s primary weapon in the middle overs for most of his career. Even during the twilight phase of his career, his effectiveness during that period has been clear. Since the 2023 World Cup, only Rashid Khan and Wanindu Hasaranga, among bowlers for Full Member nations, have taken more wickets than Rashid has between overs 11 and 40. “Those middle overs, finding ways to take wickets, that's what he's done for over 150-odd games [165] and how important he has been,” said Buttler. “No slight on anybody else, there isn't another Adil Rashid.”
 There’s no doubt that Rashid’s returns this year have been short of his best. His role in the side has been inconsistent and he will likely never reach the heights he was able to in his prime again. But that doesn’t automatically count him out of England’s World Cup squad next year.
 England’s ODI results have been volatile in the Brook era, with flashes of brilliance followed by demoralising defeats. Their current battle is getting enough pace options into the side, while also waiting on Sam Curran to produce the returns with both bat and ball they’re convinced he will. In Pakistan, and during much of the middle period of the second ODI against Australia, England’s bowling looked toothless, short of the stranglehold Rashid has previously given them. With Jacob Bethell likely to come back in when he recovers from his knee injury, and Buttler’s future to be decided, their current XI could bear little resemblance to the XI they put out in South Africa next year.
 Rashid is still England’s greatest-ever white-ball spinner, and there will likely be a time over the next 11 months where his absence becomes untenable.
